texts.orig: Objective: The study objective was to determine whether targeted therapy to optimize cerebral oxygenation is associated with improved neurocognitive and perioperative outcomes.
texts.text: Objective: The study objective was to determine whether targeted therapy to optimize cerebral oxygenation is associated with improved neurocognitive and perioperative outcomes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Methods: In a prospective trial, intraoperative cerebral oximetry monitoring using bilateral forehead probes was performed in cardiac surgical patients who were randomly assigned to an intervention group in which episodes of cerebral oxygen desaturation ( < 60 % for > 60 consecutive seconds at either probe) triggered an intervention protocol or a control group in which the cerebral oximetry data were hidden from the clinical team, and no intervention protocol was applied. Cognitive testing was performed preoperatively and at postoperative months 3 and 6; domains studied were response speed, processing speed, attention, and memory. Perioperative outcomes studied were death, hospital length of stay, intensive care unit length of stay, postoperative day of extubation, time on mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit delirium, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment on intensive care unit admission, and intensive care unit blood transfusion.

texts.orig: NIRS oximetry monitoring holds promise for guiding interventions to improve intraoperative brain oxygenation and clinical outcomes, particularly POCD. A metaanalysis of 4 randomized controlled trials performed in cardiac surgical patients found that intraoperative management guided by cerebral oximetry was associated with reduced incidence of POCD (risk ratio, 0.55; 95 % confidence interval [CI], 0.36-0.86; P ¼ .0009; I 2 ¼ 85 % ) at hospital discharge or 1 week postoperatively. 5

texts.orig: This prospective randomized controlled trial in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB investigated whether a treatment algorithm targeted to optimize intraoperative cerebral oxygenation intervention (''targeted therapy'') was associated with better neurocognitive and perioperative outcomes compared with standard care. Perioperative outcomes studied were death, hospital length of stay, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, postoperative day of extubation, time on mechanical ventilation, ICU delirium, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment on ICU admission, and ICU blood transfusion.

texts.orig: Adult patients (aged > 18 years) undergoing elective cardiac surgery requiring CPB were studied. The exclusion criteria were (1) severe preoperative cognitive impairment by history or preoperative cognitive testing; (2) sensory or motor impairment precluding reliable operation of a computer; (3) lack of access to computer-based cognitive evaluation; (4) non-English-speaking patients; (5) renal failure requiring dialysis; (6) respiratory failure requiring home oxygen use; (7) Child's B or C hepatic failure; (8) procedures with deep hypothermic circulatory arrest; and (9) baseline oximetry values less than 60 % . Eligible patients who consented to participate and met the enrollment criterion of completing preoperative cognitive testing were assigned to an intervention or control group differing with respect to rSO2 treatment algorithms (described next) by simple randomization using an online true random number generator (www.random.org).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cerebral oxygenation was monitored using the FORE-SIGHT cerebral oximeter (CAS Medical Systems, Branford, Conn), which measures absolute regional oxygen saturation using continuous-wave spatially resolved NIRS by probes placed on the forehead above the frontal lobes bilaterally (Video 1). 6,7 Oximetry monitoring was initiated in the operating room before anesthetic induction and recorded continuously every 2 seconds throughout surgery. Baseline data were obtained for the first 2 minutes after placement of the cerebral monitors before sedation while patients were breathing room air or receiving low flow rates of nasal cannula oxygen. Because the Foresight is an absolute cerebral oximeter, baseline data were obtained to ensure that the starting value for each patient was above the threshold for intervention (ie,  60 % ). Patients with baseline values less than 60 % were excluded from the study.

texts.orig: In the intervention group, the oximetry data were displayed openly to the perioperative team. The criterion for intervention was defined as rSO2 less than 60 % for more than 60 consecutive seconds at either probe. An rSO2 less than 60 % triggered an alarm, the anesthesiologist timed the event, and after 60 seconds initiated an intervention protocol similar to that of Denault and colleagues 8 until the rSO2 was restored to at least 60 % at both probes (Figure 1). For repeated cerebral desaturation episodes, the treatment algorithm was reinitiated, as appropriate to phase of care.

texts.orig: In the control group, the oximetry data were concealed from the care team by a white screen covering the monitor display. The protocol allowed for revealing the oximetry data in the event of a critically low value, defined as rSO2 less than 40 % for more than 60 seconds at either probe, that was signaled by an alarm. If the episode was expected to be transient, revealing the oximetry data and intervention would be postponed until rSO2 remained less than 40 % for more than 5 minutes. If the episode was not expected to be transient, the patient would cross over into the intervention group; rSO2 data would be revealed to the clinical team for the remainder of the operative period, and the intervention protocol would be instituted until rSO2 increased to more than 60 % .

The 2 streams of oximetry data were converted into a single stream of data by taking the lowest value at each 2-second interval (unless there was a loss of data from 1 probe). texts.orig: We conducted a prospective, randomized controlled trial in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB to test the hypothesis that optimizing cerebral oxygenation using an intraoperative NIRS monitoring-guided treatment protocol results in better neurocognitive and perioperative outcomes. For the intervention group, intraoperative cerebral oxygen desaturation (rSO2 < 60 % for > 60 consecutive seconds at either probe) triggered an intervention protocol; for the control group, the treatment team was unaware of the rSO2 data and did not apply the treatment protocol. The intervention group had a significantly better outcome in memory scores at the 6-month postoperative testing period compared with the control group. There was no association between duration or severity of intraoperative cerebral desaturation and cognitive outcome. The groups did not differ with respect to perioperative outcomes.

This implies that the treatment algorithm was an important aspect of the neuroprotection strategy, but further research is needed to indicate what specific aspects of the treatment algorithm, such as optimization of perfusion pressure, hemoglobin concentration, carbon dioxide tension, or other factors, were contributory. Regarding the clinical significance of the observed differences in cognitive outcomes, changes of this magnitude are not expected to result in significant functional deficits, although they may signal mild insults to the brain that may be avoided.

texts.orig: We chose the 60 % threshold on the basis of the previous literature examining cerebral oximetry and outcomes after cardiac surgery, in which a range of thresholds have been applied but none higher than 60 % to 65 % . 11,12,14,21-23 In addition, our own data in patients who have undergone aortic arch surgery showed statistically significant associations between desaturation duration and severe adverse outcome incidence for thresholds of 60 % and 65 % . 24 More specifically, every 10-minute increment of exposure time under the rSO2 thresholds of 60 % and 65 % was associated with increased odds of severe adverse outcome by 34.6 % (odds ratio, 1.346; 95 % CI, 1.003  1.068; P ¼ .038) and 17.4 % (odds ratio, 1.6; 95 % CI, 1.002  1.030; P ¼ .025), respectively. For this study, we defined the criterion for intervention as rSO2 less than 60 % for more than 60 consecutive seconds at either probe so as not to have an overly aggressive protocol that would have made clinical interventions too burdensome for the clinical team.

texts.orig: There were several limitations to our study. To maximize the likelihood of triggering an effective NIRS-guided treatment algorithm, we chose a mild threshold for cerebral desaturation compared with other investigations, with the goal of treating all potentially injurious cerebral desaturation episodes. As a consequence, the specificity of the defined threshold for cerebral desaturation was likely reduced, which could explain the lack of association of cerebral desaturation with outcome, because some episodes could have been clinically insignificant. As with all investigations, the NIRS data reflect saturation of cerebral tissue oxygenation from a small area of cortex within the frontal lobes, rather than brain structures that are most vulnerable to hypoxia (ie, hippocampi, watershed zones).

Although this technology allowed for long-term postoperative testing in patients who live a long distance from the tertiary care medical center, it also required that patients access the test remotely from their home computers and take the time to complete the test. Early termination of the study decreased the statistical power and prevented us from exploring potential associations of the individual components of the treatment algorithm with neurocognitive outcome. Another study limitation was the differential follow-up with postoperative cognitive testing between the intervention and control groups.

texts.orig: Intraoperative NIRS monitoring is increasingly used routinely in the anesthetic, surgical, and perfusion management during cardiac surgery. It is also used during a variety of noncardiac surgical procedures. A systematic review found that noncardiac surgical procedures associated with pronounced decreases in rSO2 are thoracic surgery involving single lung ventilation, major abdominal surgery, hip surgery, laparoscopic surgery with the patient in the reverse Trendelenburg position, shoulder arthroscopy in the beach chair position, and carotid endarterectomy with clamping of the internal carotid artery. 26 Investigations into the relationship between intraoperative cerebral oximetry and neurocognitive outcomes in noncardiac surgery have also yielded inconsistent findings. 27-35

texts.orig: For the cognitive data, raw change scores from the preoperative and postoperative time points (ie, T1 to T2, and T1 to T3) were compared between the groups using the analysis of covariance method that controlled for the baseline score. The cognitive change scores were modeled as a linear function of group assignment and baseline score; change score ¼ b 0 (intercept) þ b 1 (Intervention group) þ b 2 (baseline score). For the longitudinal data, the WGEE method was used. The models included the main effects of time (T1, T2, and T3) and group, and the time $ group interaction, adjusting for the covariates of age, gender, education level, baseline euroSCORE, CPB time, and length of hospital stay (ie, cognitive score ¼ b 0 þ b 1 [intervention group] þ b 2 [T2] þ b 3 [T3] þ b 4 [T2 $ intervention] þ b 5 [T3 $ intervention] þ covariates adjustment). A heterogeneous autoregressive structure was used for the working covariance matrix across the baseline and 3- and 6-month postoperative data; however, hypothesis testing was based on the empirical standard errors. The WGEE is often used for longitudinal data in which some subjects are lost to follow-up. Specifically, at each visit the probability for an individual to drop out at that time was estimated. The inverse of this probability was then incorporated as a numeric weight at the observation level when analyzing the data using the WGEE method. The same set of covariates as mentioned above was used to estimate the dropout probability at each visit (ie, the missingness model). Intervention effects by visit were estimated from the model based on the least-squares means. The analyses were repeated in 2 ways: (1) excluding 6 patients with more than 10 % of NIRS data that were missing and imputed, and (2) including the desaturation status and other covariates.

texts.orig: Asecondary analysis of the cognitive data was performed to evaluate the relationship between cognitive change scores and oximetry data. In this analysis, also using the WGEE method, the first step was to test the interaction between the treatment assignment and presence of cerebral desaturation. The purpose of this was to check whether the effect of intraoperative cerebral desaturation on cognitive change scores was modified by the treatment assignment, after adjusting for the covariates. If the interaction was not significant, the next step was to evaluate the independent effects of cerebral desaturation on the cognitive change scores. Last, the analysis was repeated using duration and severity of desaturation as predictors of cognitive change scores, independentofgroupassignment. P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons for the changes of 4 cognitive outcomes at each follow-up visit using the false discovery rate method. 10

Last, the analysis was repeated using duration and severity of desaturation as predictors of cognitive change scores, independentofgroupassignment. P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons for the changes of 4 cognitive outcomes at each follow-up visit using the false discovery rate method. 10
